title: Learned approximate inference extension
description: An auxiliary network can be trained to perform approximate inference by predicting z given x after the generator has finished training.
canonical_description: learn approximate posterior inference with an auxiliary network

evidence.anchor: Learned approximate inference} can be performed by training an auxiliary network
evidence.quote: \item { Learned approximate inference} can be performed by training an auxiliary network to predict

verdict.reasoning:
Two papers directly solve the gap. Paper 2 ("Improving generative adversarial network inversion via fine-tuning GAN encoders") squarely demonstrates the core idea: it takes a pre-trained, fixed GAN generator and trains an encoder (auxiliary network) to map images x back to latent codes z, using a symmetric encoder-decoder architecture with cropping attention and multi-metric loss. It validates this across StyleGANs, PGGAN, and BigGAN — concrete empirical evidence that post-hoc auxiliary inference networks work.

Paper 5 ("Generative Bayesian Inference with GANs") provides a second, independent instantiation: it trains an auxiliary conditional generator to perform approximate Bayesian posterior inference (mapping data to parameters), and after training, inference costs are negligible. This broadens the result beyond GAN inversion to general approximate inference.

The three partial_solution papers (1, 3, 4) are consistent with this picture — Paper 1 uses an auxiliary network but predicts generator offsets rather than latent codes; Papers 3 and 4 train encoders but jointly with the generator, not post-hoc. None contradict the direct solutions; they simply address adjacent problems. Together, the direct evidence confidently confirms that the gap's central claim — an auxiliary network can be trained to perform approximate inference by predicting z given x after the generator has finished training — has been validated by subsequent literature.

paper.title: Meta-Auxiliary Network for 3D GAN Inversion
paper.abstract: Real-world image manipulation has achieved fantastic progress in recent years. GAN inversion, which aims to map the real image to the latent code faithfully, is the first step in this pipeline. However, existing GAN inversion methods fail to achieve high reconstruction quality and fast inference at the same time. In addition, existing methods are built on 2D GANs and lack explicitly mechanisms to enforce multi-view consistency.In this work, we present a novel meta-auxiliary framework, while leveraging the newly developed 3D GANs as generator. The proposed method adopts a two-stage strategy. In the first stage, we invert the input image to an editable latent code using off-the-shelf inversion techniques. The auxiliary network is proposed to refine the generator parameters with the given image as input, which both predicts offsets for weights of convolutional layers and sampling positions of volume rendering. In the second stage, we perform meta-learning to fast adapt the auxiliary network to the input image, then the final reconstructed image is synthesized via the meta-learned auxiliary network. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves better performances on both inversion and editing tasks.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes an auxiliary network that takes an input image x and predicts offsets to a pre-trained 3D GAN generator's parameters (convolutional weights and volume rendering sampling positions) to improve reconstruction quality. This is related to the gap of "learned approximate inference with an auxiliary network" in that the auxiliary network performs a form of inference (predicting how to modify the generator given x). However, the auxiliary network does NOT predict the latent code z given x — instead, it predicts generator parameter offsets, while the latent code is obtained separately via an off-the-shelf encoder. The paper also incorporates meta-learning (MAML) to enable fast test-time adaptation of the auxiliary network.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically asks about learning approximate posterior inference by predicting z (the latent code) given x using an auxiliary network. This paper does NOT address that: its auxiliary network predicts generator parameter offsets (weight residuals and coordinate deformations), not the latent code. The latent code is obtained from a separate off-the-shelf encoder and is not learned by the auxiliary network. The core problem of learning an auxiliary network that performs amortized inference over latents (z|x) remains unaddressed. Additionally, this paper is specific to GAN inversion for 3D-aware GANs (EG3D), not general approximate posterior inference.
evidence_snippets: In the first stage, we invert the input image to an editable latent code using off-the-shelf inversion techniques. The auxiliary network is proposed to refine the generator parameters with the given image as input, which both predicts offsets for weights of convolutional layers and sampling positions of volume rendering.

To achieve our goal of minimizing the objective defined in Eq. [REF:equ:target], we introduce an auxiliary network $Aux$ that is responsible for predicting a new set of parameters $\hat{\theta}^G$ for generator $G$.
The input of our method includes an image $x$, a generator $G$ with parameters $\theta^G$, and an initial inverted latent code $\hat{\omega}_{init}$, which is obtained using an off-the-shelf encoder.

paper.title: Improving generative adversarial network inversion via fine-tuning GAN encoders
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can synthesize high-quality (HQ) images, and GAN inversion is a technique that discovers how to invert given images back to latent space. While existing methods perform on StyleGAN inversion, they have limited performance and are not generalized to different GANs. To address these issues, we proposed a self-supervised method to pre-train and fine-tune GAN encoders. First, we designed an adaptive block to fit different encoder architectures for inverting diverse GANs. Then we pre-train GAN encoders using synthesized images and emphasize local regions through cropping images. Finally, we fine-tune the pre-trained GAN encoder for inverting real images. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, our method achieved better results that reconstructed high-quality images on mainstream GANs. Our code and pre-trained models are available at: https://github.com/disanda/Deep-GAN-Encoders.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes a method for GAN inversion by training an encoder network (auxiliary network) that maps images back to latent codes after the GAN generator has been pre-trained. The method uses a symmetric encoder-decoder architecture with an adaptive block to match different GAN generators (StyleGANs, PGGAN, BigGAN), pre-trains the encoder on synthesized images, and fine-tunes it on real images. It incorporates cropping attention and a multi-metric loss function (MSE, COS, LPIPS, SSIM) to improve reconstruction quality. This directly demonstrates the concept of learning approximate posterior inference with an auxiliary network after generator training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of training an auxiliary network for approximate inference (predicting z given x) after the generator has finished training. It demonstrates this approach works across multiple GAN architectures. The gap is a general methodological statement, and this paper provides a concrete instantiation of it. No part of the gap remains open — the paper shows exactly this approach can be implemented and works effectively.
evidence_snippets: We transform pre-trained GAN into an auto-encoder, an encoder-decoder architecture. Next, we regard pre-trained generators as decoders and design corresponding encoders in GANs.
Training the encoder aims to invert synthesized images to the latent space and reconstruct these images using the encoded latent vectors, i.e., $\mathbf{x} \simeq \mathbf{x'}$

Fine-tuned GAN encoders can find latent vectors that faithfully reconstruct real images. Fine-tuning improves the capacity of encoders to represent real image features that differ significantly from the pre-training datasets.

paper.title: IVE-GAN: Invariant Encoding Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a powerful framework for generative tasks. However, they are difficult to train and tend to miss modes of the true data generation process. Although GANs can learn a rich representation of the covered modes of the data in their latent space, the framework misses an inverse mapping from data to this latent space. We propose Invariant Encoding Generative Adversarial Networks (IVE-GANs), a novel GAN framework that introduces such a mapping for individual samples from the data by utilizing features in the data which are invariant to certain transformations. Since the model maps individual samples to the latent space, it naturally encourages the generator to cover all modes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of generative performance and learning rich representations on several datasets including common benchmark image generation tasks.

assessments.contribution_summary: IVE-GAN introduces an encoder network E that maps data samples x to a latent representation z, which is exactly the kind of approximate inference network described in the gap. The encoder is trained adversarially alongside the generator and discriminator, using invariant transformations to encourage rich latent representations. The paper demonstrates that the encoder learns meaningful latent embeddings that can reconstruct inputs and enable interpolation between real data points.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically describes training an auxiliary network to perform approximate inference "after the generator has finished training" — a sequential/post-hoc approach where the generator is first trained and then fixed, and only afterward is an inference network trained to invert it. IVE-GAN instead trains the encoder jointly with the generator in an end-to-end adversarial framework. This means the encoder influences generator training and vice versa, which is a fundamentally different setup. The paper does not address whether a separately trained inference network can be effectively learned after a pre-trained, fixed generator, nor does it compare the joint vs. post-hoc training paradigms for inference quality.
evidence_snippets: We propose a novel GAN framework, Invariant-Encoding Generative Adversarial Networks (IVE-GAN), which extends the classical GAN architecture by an additional encoding unit $\mathbf{E}$ to map samples from the true data $\mathbf{x}$ to the latent space $\mathbf{z}$

paper.title: O-GAN: Extremely Concise Approach for Auto-Encoding Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: In this paper, we propose Orthogonal Generative Adversarial Networks (O-GANs). We decompose the network of discriminator orthogonally and add an extra loss into the objective of common GANs, which can enforce discriminator become an effective encoder. The same extra loss can be embedded into any kind of GANs and there is almost no increase in computation. Furthermore, we discuss the principle of our method, which is relative to the fully-exploiting of the remaining degrees of freedom of discriminator. As we know, our solution is the simplest approach to train a generative adversarial network with auto-encoding ability.

assessments.contribution_summary: O-GAN proposes a method to make the discriminator in a GAN also function as an encoder by decomposing it orthogonally and adding a Pearson correlation loss between latent codes z and their reconstructions E(G(z)). This enables the discriminator to perform approximate inference (mapping images x to latent codes z). However, the encoder is trained jointly with the generator from the start, not as a separate auxiliary network trained after the generator has finished training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically describes training an auxiliary network to perform approximate inference *after* the generator has finished training. O-GAN instead trains the encoder jointly with the generator from the beginning as part of the adversarial process. The paper does not address the scenario where one has a pre-trained, fixed generator and then trains a separate inference network post-hoc. The encoder in O-GAN is also not a separate auxiliary network — it is the discriminator itself, decomposed and trained simultaneously with the generator. The gap about post-hoc auxiliary inference networks remains open.
evidence_snippets: We decompose the network of discriminator orthogonally and add an extra loss into the objective of common GANs, which can enforce discriminator become an effective encoder.

We develop a extra objective function for common GANs, and with this extra term the discriminator can not only distinguish whether the input image is real or not but also have ability to extract good features for the input image.
We train [REF:eq:simplest-2] with one E steps per G step.

paper.title: Generative Bayesian Inference with GANs
paper.abstract: In the absence of explicit or tractable likelihoods, Bayesians often resort to approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) for inference. Our work bridges ABC with deep neural implicit samplers based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and adversarial variational Bayes. Both ABC and GANs compare aspects of observed and fake data to simulate from posteriors and likelihoods, respectively. We develop a Bayesian GAN (B-GAN) sampler that directly targets the posterior by solving an adversarial optimization problem. B-GAN is driven by a deterministic mapping learned on the ABC reference by conditional GANs. Once the mapping has been trained, iid posterior samples are obtained by filtering noise at a negligible additional cost. We propose two post-processing local refinements using (1) data-driven proposals with importance reweighting, and (2) variational Bayes. We support our findings with frequentist-Bayesian results, showing that the typical total variation distance between the true and approximate posteriors converges to zero for certain neural network generators and discriminators. Our findings on simulated data show highly competitive performance relative to some of the most recent likelihood-free posterior simulators.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes B-GAN, a conditional GAN framework that trains an auxiliary neural network (generator) to perform approximate Bayesian posterior inference. The generator learns an implicit mapping g_β(Z, X) → θ from noise and data to parameters, trained on an ABC reference table. Once trained, for any observed data X₀, posterior samples are obtained at negligible cost by simply passing noise through the generator: θ̃ = g_β(Z, X₀). This directly implements the idea of training an auxiliary network for approximate inference that can be used after training is complete.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap: it trains an auxiliary network (the conditional GAN generator) to perform approximate posterior inference, and after training, inference is obtained by feeding noise through the trained network. The paper provides both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation. No part of the gap remains unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: Once the mapping has been trained, iid posterior samples are obtained by filtering noise at a negligible additional cost.
Our B-GAN sampler uses contrastive learning to estimate the conditional distribution π(θ|X) for any X.
One of the practical appeals of this sampling procedure is that, once the generator has been trained, the simulation cost is negligible.
